item.title: 30-year wait ends for human rights
item.description: Papua New Guinea’s Department of Justice and Attorney-General [DJAG] has launched the long-awaited National Human Rights Policy in Port Moresby, ending a nearly 30-year wait for a national oversight framework. The human rights policy was launched in partnership with the European Union [EU] and the United Nations [UN].
item.content:encoded:
Papua New Guinea’s Department of Justice and Attorney-General [DJAG] has launched the long-awaited National Human Rights Policy in Port Moresby, ending a nearly 30-year wait for a national oversight framework.

The human rights policy was launched in partnership with the European Union [EU] and the United Nations [UN].

The policy aims to translate constitutional guarantees into practical protections for citizens across the country, with a focus on law and order, gender-based violence [GBV], land rights, and access to public services.

EU Ambassador to PNG, Erica Hasznos said the policy was the result of an inclusive consultative process involving civil society, churches, traditional leaders, and state agencies.

“This is a very important day in the sense that we have a human rights policy in place,” Hasznos said.

“It is good to have a policy, but it is even better to have action based on this policy. The EU will stand by Papua New Guinea as a committed partner to turn this policy into real action.”

Hasznos said the EU has committed K7 million in direct support for human rights projects.

This includes funding to draft constitutional amendments, set up the future National Human Rights Commission, and support the ongoing K50 million EU Spotlight Initiative targeting gender-based violence.

UN Resident Coordinator Shalini Bahuguna commended the Marape-Rosso government for taking a whole of government and society approach to address human rights issues.

“The Constitution of Papua New Guinea is amongst the world’s strongest in terms of human rights protection,” Bahuguna said.

“This policy translates those constitutional guarantees into real, practical results for people, whether children can attend school, women are protected from violence, or communities can access justice.”

Bahuguna said the real work now moves to implementation at the provincial, district, and ward levels.

DJAG Deputy Secretary for Legal Policy, E’ava Geita said the department accepts the responsibility of leading the national implementation.

Geita outlined DJAG's four strategic pillars under the plan:

Establishing the National Human Rights Commission; Building institutional capacity across state agencies; Fostering cross-sectoral partnerships; and, Enforcing strict monitoring through a National Mechanism for Implementation, Reporting, and Follow-up [NMIRF].

“This has been a long and arduous journey spanning over three decades,” Geita said. “With the formal launch of this policy, our focus shifts decisively from design to rigorous implementation.”

item.title: Appeal for greater maritime safety in Madang Province
item.description: A concerned senior citizen on Madang's Karkar Island is calling for greater maritime safety in the province. Tony Dibul, a former captain in the PNG Defence Force, made the call this week following the recent sea mishaps in the country's maritime provinces.
item.content:encoded:
A concerned senior citizen on Madang's Karkar Island is calling for greater maritime safety in the province.

Tony Dibul, a former captain in the PNG Defence Force, made the call this week following the recent sea mishaps in the country's maritime provinces.

"As an ordinary citizen who has travelled extensively by small craft throughout Madang Province over many years, I feel compelled to speak out on an issue that continues to put unnecessary lives at risk.

"Far too many boat operators continue to ignore maritime safety advisories, weather broadcasts, and the most basic safety requirements before putting to sea. This attitude is becoming increasingly dangerous and unacceptable," he said.

Just this past weekend, one dinghy carrying eight persons on board submerged and drifted from Saidor to Vidar before those on board were rescued. In another separate incident, another dinghy capsized outside Vidar.

Mr Dibul added, "Thankfully, no lives were lost in either incident, but that should not give us comfort. Instead, it should serve as a serious warning.

He said every one of these incidents trigger search and rescue operations involving volunteers, government agencies, and other boat operators who willingly risk their own lives to save others.

Mr Dibul further stated that these operations consume valuable time, fuel, equipment, and public resources. They expose rescuers to the very same dangerous sea conditions that caused the emergency in the first place.

The question we must ask ourselves is simple.

How many more warnings and near tragedies will it take before we change our attitude towards maritime safety?

"I commend the Madang Provincial Small Craft Registry Board for the progress it has made in registering small craft throughout the province. Registration is an important step towards improving maritime safety.

"However, registration alone is not enough.

"The Board, together with the responsible maritime authorities, must now place equal emphasis on enforcing the safety requirements that accompany registration.

"Compliance with maritime safety standards should not be treated as optional," he emphasised.

He said boat operators who continue to ignore weather and sea condition warnings, overload their vessels beyond safe carrying capacity, operate without sufficient life jackets for every passenger, fail to carry the required safety equipment, and operate vessels that do not comply with safety requirements should be prevented from departing.

"Where operators deliberately disregard these requirements and place lives at risk, the relevant authorities should not hesitate to prosecute offenders under the applicable maritime laws.

"Saving lives must take precedence over convenience or commercial gain," Dibul stated.

To passengers, Mr Dibul said that they also have a responsibility.

"Do not board a boat that is overloaded. Do not board a vessel that lacks life jackets or appears unsafe. If weather conditions are poor, postpone your journey. No appointment, cargo, or fare is worth a human life.

"For too long, we have accepted preventable maritime incidents as part of life along our coastline. They are not. Most of these incidents can be avoided if operators obey the law, respect the sea, and put safety first, he stressed.

Dibul clarified that he made this appeal not to criticise anyone but because he has witnessed too many unnecessary emergencies and too many rescue operations that could have been avoided.

"The sea will always command our respect. It does not forgive complacency, carelessness, or ignorance.

He appealed to everyone, including boat owners, operators, passengers, and authorities, to work together in order to ensure that every voyage begins safely and ends safely.

"One preventable death at sea is one too many," he said.

item.title: Tukana returns home as free community screenings tour Bougainville

From there, screenings will travel to Hutjena in Buka on July 31, Arawa Independence Park on August 1,
item.content:encoded:
One of Papua New Guinea's most celebrated films, Tukana – Husat I Asua, is returning to the big screen in Bougainville, with a series of free community screenings beginning on Wednesday, July 30.

The tour will open in Tinputz, the home of the late Albert Toro, whose life inspired the iconic film. From there, screenings will travel to Hutjena in Buka on July 31, Arawa Independence Park on August 1, and conclude at the Mamaromino Women's Resource Centre in Buin on August 3.

Set in Bougainville, Tukana tells a compelling story of tradition, identity, leadership, and social change. Since its original release in the 1980s, the film has become a landmark in Papua New Guinea's cinematic history, resonating with audiences across generations.

The community screenings aim to bring people together to celebrate Bougainville's rich cultural heritage while introducing the restored classic to a new generation of viewers.

The film was recently digitally restored by the Papua New Guinea National Film Institute [NFI] in partnership with the Australian National Film and Sound Archive and Spectrum Films. The restoration was presented as a gift from the Australian Government to Papua New Guinea to commemorate the country's 50th Independence Anniversary.

The Bougainville screening tour is a joint initiative of the PNG National Film Institute and the Bougainville Arts, Culture and Tourism Authority. The program is supported by the Governments of Australia and New Zealand as part of their ongoing partnership with the Autonomous Bougainville Government to preserve and promote Bougainville's arts, culture and identity.

All screenings are free and open to the public.

item.title: Water provided for government institutions and communities in Tari
item.description: Two 10,000-litre water trucks are now operational in Tari, delivering emergency water to critical institutions and communities affected by the prolonged El Niño drought. The trucks are on the road daily, visiting schools, health facilities, churches, and communities to refill water tanks and containers.
item.content:encoded:
Two 10,000-litre water trucks are now operational in Tari, delivering emergency water to critical institutions and communities affected by the prolonged El Niño drought.

The trucks are on the road daily, visiting schools, health facilities, churches, and communities to refill water tanks and containers.

The drought has devastated communities across the country. In Hela, all small creeks have dried up, leaving many families without access to safe water.

Hela Governor Philip Undialu said the water trucks are part of the Provincial Government’s immediate response. He also announced that additional water trucks and a specialised water drilling rig are expected to arrive soon.

"The Hela Provincial Government will continue investing in sustainable water infrastructure to safeguard our communities from the impacts of the El Niño drought and from future disasters," he said.

Governor Undialu recently announced the successful activation of Hela Province’s first bore water system under the government’s El Niño preparedness and emergency water response plan.

The reactivated bore will provide a reliable source of clean water for Tari Hospital, Tari Township, and surrounding communities throughout the current dry spell.

The Governor thanked the China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation, CCECC, for its technical support in restoring the bore system.

"I thank CCECC for its valuable support. Their contribution has strengthened Hela’s emergency response capacity and will ensure our hospital and town have water security during this drought," he stated.

He stressed that the bore project and the incoming drilling rig will expand groundwater access across the province, reducing reliance on surface water sources that dry up during El Niño.

He said water security will remain a priority as Hela prepares for more frequent climate-related disasters.

item.title: 14 criminal appeals before Supreme Court in historic Vanimo Sitting
item.description: The Supreme Court of Papua New Guinea is currently hearing 14 criminal appeals in Vanimo this week. This marks the first time in 50 years that the Supreme Court circuit has sat in Vanimo, bringing the country’s highest court closer to the people of West Sepik.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court of Papua New Guinea is currently hearing 14 criminal appeals in Vanimo this week.

This marks the first time in 50 years that the Supreme Court circuit has sat in Vanimo, bringing the country’s highest court closer to the people of West Sepik.

Speaking to NBC News, Public Solicitor of Papua New Guinea, Leslie Mamu confirmed that all 14 cases are now before the Supreme Court judges, with final judgments expected by Friday.

Mr. Mamu said the matters before the court are appeals, where appellants are challenging decisions of the National Court on both conviction and sentencing.

“The judges will deliberate after all hearings are completed and deliver their decisions. Appellants should have the court’s decision by the end of this week,” Mr. Mamu said.

Hearings commenced on Monday and continued through Wednesday.

Of the 14 cases listed, 13 relate to murder and manslaughter. The remaining case involves Child Sexual Penetration.

One of the appellants, Child Sexual Penetration convict Darren Babia, is challenging both his conviction and 20-year prison sentence handed down by the National Court.

Mr. Babia has filed a formal appeal against the National Court’s decision.

Justice Colin Makail earlier told the court that out of 1,196 Supreme Court cases nationwide, only 15 originated from West Sepik, a figure he said reflects a largely law-abiding population in the province.

The Supreme Court is expected to deliver all judgments on Friday.

item.title: Governor Allan Bird urged to address hardship from boundary shift
item.description: Villagers in Angoram are appealing directly to East Sepik Governor Allan Bird to intervene in the ongoing dispute over the newly created Middle Sepik electoral boundary, warning that the changes will bring hardship to their people. Community spokesperson Libert Sangundi said the boundary shift has left families anxious about losing access to services and representation they have relied on for deca
item.content:encoded:
Villagers in Angoram are appealing directly to East Sepik Governor Allan Bird to intervene in the ongoing dispute over the newly created Middle Sepik electoral boundary, warning that the changes will bring hardship to their people.

Community spokesperson Libert Sangundi said the boundary shift has left families anxious about losing access to services and representation they have relied on for decades.

"Our people are worried that being moved into a new district without consultation will make it harder to access government services, schools, health facilities and even basic infrastructure support," Sangundi explained. "We are calling on Governor Bird to hear our concerns and ensure that our voices are not ignored."

The Kanda communities argue that the decision to place their customary land into the Middle Sepik District was made without adequate consultation, despite petitions submitted last year and again in March 2026.

They say the lack of response from authorities has deepened frustration and uncertainty.

Villagers fear that the boundary change could disrupt their livelihoods, especially those who depend on Angoram Station for trade, transport and administrative services.

Sangundi noted that many families already face challenges with road access, market opportunities and health care, and the boundary shift risks worsening these conditions.

"We are not opposing reforms, but we want to understand why our people were moved without being consulted. If this decision stands, it will create unnecessary hardship for ordinary families who depend on Angoram for survival," he said. The communities are urging Governor Bird to step in and facilitate dialogue between the Electoral Boundaries Commission, the Angoram District Development Authority and the affected villages.

They say his leadership is critical to restoring trust and ensuring that development priorities are not undermined by administrative changes.

NBC News is in communication with relevant stakeholders to gather their responses regarding the unrest and the concerns raised by the Kanda communities. Their comments had not been received at the time of publication.

item.title: Ex- Malala students bid farewell to Sr. Edith after 50 plus years of service
item.description: Former students of Malala Catholic Secondary School in Madang gathered last Sunday morning at the Alexsishaffen SSPS Convent Chapel to celebrate a farewell Holy Mass in honour of one of the school's founding sisters, Sr. Edith Cornelia Ties. Sr. Edith, a member of the SSPS Sisters congregation, dedicated over 50 years of service as a teacher in Madang Province, including 30 years at Malala Catholi
item.content:encoded:
Former students of Malala Catholic Secondary School in Madang gathered last Sunday morning at the Alexsishaffen SSPS Convent Chapel to celebrate a farewell Holy Mass in honour of one of the school's founding sisters, Sr. Edith Cornelia Ties.

Sr. Edith, a member of the SSPS Sisters congregation, dedicated over 50 years of service as a teacher in Madang Province, including 30 years at Malala Catholic Secondary School.

She also served for six years as Provincial Superior at Divine Word High School, later known as Divine Word Institute and now Divine Word University.

The farewell Mass brought together a large number of former students whose lives were shaped by Sr. Edith's commitment to education, faith, and service.

During the homily, celebrant Fr. Willson Jacob thanked God for Sr. Edith's life and service. He reflected on the example of King Solomon, who asked God for wisdom.

‘’A true servant of God is one who seeks wisdom and faithfully serves others, with a listening heart and serves truthfully," he said.

Former students described Sr. Edith as a dedicated, humble, and respectful educator who earned the respect of both past and present students.

Nicholas Gamuna, who is now a student leader at DWU, said that Sr. Edith's commitment to discipline, compassion, and education has left a lasting impact on generations of Malala students.

Responding to the heartfelt tributes, Sr. Edith thanked her former students and said that respect is something that is earned through the way people treat one another.

She added that teaching and spending time with her students has been the most precious part of her ministry, saying it is a calling she has deeply loved.

“I love teaching. On the weekends, I have body aches, but on Monday, when I stepped into the classroom, there are no aches at all. All my students, past and present, are well behaved. This is the most thing I treasured and I will take it with me home to Austria. I pray that God continue to bless all my students, their children, and grandchildren," she said.

The farewell mass was an emotional occasion as former students reflected on the lasting impact Sr. Edith has had on their lives, not only academically but also spiritually and personally.

Originally from Austria, Sr. Edith left her home in her early twenties to serve as a missionary in Papua New Guinea. She is one of the four founding sisters of Malala Catholic Secondary School.

Two other sisters have since passed on while the only one remaining is sister, Sr. Ingeburg is continuing her ministry at Malala.

item.content:encoded:
A community Tari-Pori district of Hela has established the Hayapuga Construction Company in a bid to create jobs, support local institutions, and keep youths away from illegal activities.

Inspired by former United States President John F. Kennedy’s call to; "Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country", local leaders say the new company in Hayapuga community, is about taking ownership of its own development through Small to Medium Enterprises [SME] participation.

Leading the initiative is Steven Talu Halimbu. He said the purpose of the company is to give locals direct opportunities in building and construction.

"The company is for the Halimbu community and for Hayapuga as a whole. We are starting small to ensure churches and schools are given assistance first. We cannot always expect the Government to do everything for us."

Halimbu and other like-minded leaders have previously supported churches, schools, and youth empowerment programs. The new company will expand that work by assisting with the construction and maintenance of church buildings, classrooms, and market facilities where people can sell their garden produce.

"We put God first in everything we do. This company is for the people. We start small and through the grace of God, we expect to expand," Mr. Halimbu said.

He also appealed for unity across the LLG.

"Everyone in Hayapuga must support the work of churches and schools. When we work together, development will follow."

Halimbu said many educated people from Hela have been living outside the province due to law and order problems. With peace slowly restoring in parts of Hayapuga, he is optimistic they will return.

"Many of our educated elites left because of lawlessness. Today there is peace. If they see that we are living peacefully and participating in meaningful activities, they will come back to be with us," he said.

Another local leader, Tobby Maya Pajape, is also driving change in the Karai area. He is leading the opening of bank accounts for women and youth groups to enable them to participate in SMEs.

"All we want is for the people to settle and meaningfully participate in local SMEs and live peaceful lives. I urge our youths to embrace development changes and take part in church and community activities,” he said.

item.title: LOs demand K5.5mil compensation as water main repairs blocked
item.description: The proposed partial shutdown of Port Moresby’s water supply faces delays after landowners blocked access to the damaged main pipeline, demanding K5.5 million in compensation.
